author: Baron Godfrey Rathbone Benson Charnwood
claims: The secession of South Carolina was not a movement that could be immediately quelled by prompt repressive measures.
Lincoln's administration was prepared to defend other forts, such as Fort Pickens on the Gulf of Mexico.
Lincoln reserved his judgment on the Fort Sumter situation for a considerable period.
Lincoln declared he would take no provocative step regarding the secession crisis.
Seward proposed a program that suggested he should control all policy.
Lincoln decided to send provisions, but not troops, to Fort Sumter.
The decision to send provisions to Fort Sumter was made after Senators and Congressmen indicated Northern opinion would support it.
The decision to send provisions to Fort Sumter was taken perilously late, exposing the government to the risk of humiliation.
Jefferson Davis ordered Beauregard to reduce Fort Sumter.
Confederate batteries opened fire on Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861.
Fort Sumter became untenable on April 13, 1861.
Anderson capitulated on April 14, 1861, marching out with the honors of war.
The Union flag was fired upon by Confederates, leading the North to spring to arms.
Following the bombardment of Fort Sumter, President Lincoln issued a Proclamation calling for 75,000 militia men.
The affair of Fort Sumter and Lincoln's Proclamation aroused and concentrated public opinion in the free Northern States and in the seceded States.
President Jefferson Davis had more than double the number of the United States Army at his command before any shots were fired at Fort Sumter.
On April 14, 1865, the Union flag was hoisted again on Fort Sumter by General Anderson.
